newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar off high by late Tokyo, but well-supported.
newsitem.headline: Dollar off high by late Tokyo, but well-supported.

text.p: 0639 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT
The dollar fell from its peak against the yen and the mark by late Tokyo trade on Tuesday, but was well-supported on demand for the greenback on falls.

Dealers said the dollar lost ground after reaching its high of 114.57 yen on sales by Japanese exporters and hedge-linked sales by institutional investors, but the greenback found solid support at around 114.00 yen on purchases by U.S. hedge funds.
The greenback fell slightly below 1.79 marks by late trade as speculative sales intensified on vague rumours that the Bundesbank might be checking rates, dealers said.
Such rumours weighed on the dollar, but many dealers were sceptical that the central bank would take such action.

"If the Bundesbank actually stepped into the market, then we would see the dollar falling more sharply. The extent of the falls is not big enough to back up speculation of the rate checks or intervention," a Japanese city bank dealer said.
The mark was also bought back against the yen, although the German currency's recovery was limited, dealers said.

Another dealer said some German banks sold the greenback against the mark in large amounts in early European trading. Some speculators were intentionally spreading the rumour of the rate check on the back of such large sales.
The dollar was well-supported above 114 yen, but operators' attention was fixed on movements in the dollar/mark rate.

"Selling pressure by exporters and life insurers intensified when the dollar rose towards 114.50 yen, but the dollar's bullishness against the mark is providing firm support to the dollar/yen," a Japanese commercial bank dealer said.

The dollar edged higher against the yen in late morning trade in reaction to reported remarks by senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara that were dollar supportive, but the dollar's rise was short-lived, dealers said. His comments prompted a slew of short-covering and set off stop-loss buying, they said.

Sakakibara was quoted by a foreign wire service as saying that the foreign exchange market has excessive expectations of the yen's appreciation, which are not justified, and that Japan and the rest of the Group of Seven (G7) nations have no intention of using foreign exchange rates as a trade tool.
The market is waiting for a news briefing by Sakakibara at 6.30 p.m. (0930 GMT) after his official appointment to the post of vice finance minister for international affairs.
The outgoing MOF vice minister for international affairs, Takatoshi Kato, will also attend the news briefing.
But a second Japanese city bank dealer said: "We are focusing on the news briefing, but I doubt that he will comment on the forex market because the news briefing is on his new appointment."
